issues.title: Off-by-one index in the old batch-space update

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $V_n\subset X$ be some subspace of dimension $n\in\N$.

issues.failure_explanation: The paper declares that \(V_n\) has dimension \(n\). For an independent batch, the displayed update adds \(b\) vectors to \(V_{b\ell}\), so its intended dimension is \(b\ell+b=b(\ell+1)=\widetilde n+1\). Nevertheless, it is assigned to \(V_{\widetilde n}\). In the following iteration, \(\undertilde n'=b(\ell+1)=\widetilde n+1\), so the required \(V_{\undertilde n'}\) is undefined. Dependence within a batch creates a separate quality defect but does not remove this indexing contradiction, which already occurs for independent snapshots.
issues.overall_effect: As written, the algorithm does not provide the space required by its next iteration and does not satisfy the dimension convention used throughout the subsequent matrix analysis.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace both end-of-batch occurrences of \(V_{\widetilde n}\) by \(V_{\widetilde n+1}\), so the update reads \(V_{\widetilde n+1}:=\operatorname{span}(V_{\undertilde n}\oplus\{f_{\undertilde n},\ldots,f_{\widetilde n}\})\), and orthogonalize that same space.
issues.why_classification: The batch contains exactly \(b\) indices, so \(\undertilde n+b=\widetilde n+1\), which is also the next iteration's value of \(\undertilde n\). The dimension convention and subsequent use of the spaces uniquely force this off-by-one correction; no mathematical inference or construction must be changed for this indexing root.

issues.title: Stale within-batch selections invalidate the diagonal lower bound
issues.failure_explanation: The lemma claims \(\gamma\sigma_{n+b-1}\leq |a_{n,n}|=\sigma_n(f_n)\) for every batch member, but only the first member satisfies a weak-greedy condition. The others are selected using \(r_{\undertilde n}\), before preceding batch members are incorporated. For a concrete admissible example, take \(b=2\), \(\gamma=1\), \(r_n=\sigma_n\), \(X=\mathbb R^3\), and \(\mathcal F=\{e_1,0.9e_1+\varepsilon e_2,0.5e_3\}\) with \(0<\varepsilon<0.5\). The first batch selects the first two elements by their norms. Under the uniquely intended sequential space convention, the second diagonal entry is \(\varepsilon\), while \(\sigma_2=0.5\), contradicting the claimed bound for \(n=1\). Thus even linear independence does not rescue the stale-surrogate argument.
issues.overall_effect: The principal matrix property fails in both the Hilbert and Banach analyses. Hence the product estimates and all subsequent algebraic and exponential convergence-rate transfers for the old unfiltered batch algorithm are not established.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Retain the unfiltered batch algorithm but replace the full-row matrix lemma by a batch-boundary version. Let \(W_\ell\) be the space before batch \(\ell\), let \(\tau_\ell=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\operatorname{dist}(f,W_\ell)\), and let \(g_\ell\) be the first member of that batch. Then \(\operatorname{dist}(g_\ell,W_\ell)\geq\gamma\tau_\ell\). Applying the existing determinant argument to the matrix formed from the normalized residuals of the \(g_\ell\), and the analogous norming-functional construction in Banach spaces, gives convergence in the effective greedy index \(\ell\). Restate all listed rates using \(\lfloor n/b\rfloor\) (or the number of completed batches), with the resulting \(b\)-dependent constants and exponential coefficient, rather than claiming a diagonal bound for every stale batch member.
issues.why_classification: The counterexample rules out a local repair of the asserted lower bound for all batch members. The batch-boundary argument is nevertheless a concrete, contained bypass using the paper's existing triangular-matrix architecture: arbitrary stale members act only as additional enrichment, while each first member has the required weak-greedy property. It preserves the old algorithm, parallel batch selection, and comparable polynomial and stretched-exponential convergence orders, but requires a nontrivial replacement lemma and a limited \(b\)-dependent weakening throughout the Hilbert and Banach chains. It is therefore moderate rather than minor or serious.

issues.title: Index-dependent constants are treated as fixed in the rate proof
issues.failure_explanation: If \(M\) is the first failure of the polynomial statement, minimality gives \(\sigma_{2s}\leq C_1(2s,b)(2s)^{-\alpha}\). The proof instead uses the same \(C_1\) as at \(M\). Since the paper itself notes that \(C_1(n,b)\) decreases with \(n\), one generally has \(C_1(2s,b)\geq C_1(M,b)\), so the required stronger estimate does not follow. The exponential cases similarly compare a target value \(c_1(M,b)\) with ceilings evaluated at the auxiliary index \(s\), although \(c_1(n,b)\) increases with \(n\). Thus parts (ii) and (iii) are not proved with their displayed index-dependent constants.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed polynomial and exponential transfer rates with the sharpened target-dependent constants are unsupported. The same asymptotic orders can still be obtained with conservative constants fixed in the induction index.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Choose the constants before starting each induction and use those same constants at the failure index and every auxiliary index. A direct conservative choice is \(\overline C_1(b)=\max\{C_0 2^{\alpha+1}\gamma^{-2}(b+3)^{2\alpha},(b+2)^\alpha\}\) and \(\overline c_1(b)=\min\{c_0 2^{-(\alpha+1)}(b+1)^{-\alpha},(\ln C_1)b^{-\alpha}\}\). Rerun the existing contradiction arguments with these fixed values, remove the unsupported claim that the constants sharpen with the target index, and propagate the fixed constants through Corollary \(\mathrm{Cor{:}expDecay}\).
issues.why_classification: Minimality at \(M\) supplies only the bound with the constant evaluated at the smaller auxiliary index, so the displayed inference cannot be repaired by a notational edit. Uniform conservative constants give a contained and source-supported repair with the same hypotheses and polynomial or stretched-exponential orders. They do, however, surrender the advertised target-dependent sharpening, including a quantitatively meaningful exponential-rate coefficient, so the repair is a limited weakening rather than a no-loss minor correction.

issues.title: The exact exponential-rate ratio ignores the active minimum branches
issues.failure_explanation: For \(n\geq b\geq2\), the first branches are \(A=c_0 4^{-\alpha}/2\) for \(b=1\) and \(B=c_0 6^{-\alpha}/2=(2/3)^\alpha A\) for the batch case. The actual definitions are \(c_1(n,1)=\min\{A,\ln C_1\}\) and \(c_1(n,b)=\min\{B,(\ln C_1)b^{-\alpha}\}\). The proof simply asserts the first-branch values. For example, with \(\alpha=1\), \(b=2\), \(c_0=1\), \(\gamma=1\), and \(C_0=e^{0.02}/2\), one has \(\ln C_1=0.01\), so the two constants are \(0.01\) and \(0.005\), whereas the claimed ratio gives \(0.006\overline6\). These parameters are admissible, and even the zero compact set satisfies the width hypothesis.
issues.overall_effect: The universal exact rate-loss factor and the downstream interpretation based on replacing \(n\) by \(2n/3\) are unsupported. Only the separately defined minimum-based convergence constants remain available.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Retain the actual minimum formulas. With \(A=c_0 4^{-\alpha}/2\), \(x=\ln C_1\), and \(r=(2/3)^\alpha\), state \(c_1(n,1)=\min\{A,x\}\) and \(c_1(n,b)=\min\{rA,b^{-\alpha}x\}\). For positive rate constants this yields \(b^{-\alpha}c_1(n,1)\leq c_1(n,b)\leq r c_1(n,1)\). The asserted equality with factor \(r\) should be restricted to the case \(b^{-\alpha}x\geq rA\), when the first branches are active, and the unconditional interpretation as replacing \(n\) by \(2n/3\) should be removed.
issues.why_classification: The correction is algebraically local and leaves the underlying minimum-based convergence estimate intact. However, the logarithmic branches are active for a natural admissible set of parameters, not merely an exceptional degeneracy, and in that regime the corollary's principal universal exact factor is false. Replacing it by a conditional equality and universal bounds is a meaningful but limited weakening of a recognizably comparable rate-comparison result, hence a moderate issue.

issues.title: Reversed inequality in the Banach exponential case split
issues.failure_explanation: Let \(L=\lceil2+(b-1)/s\rceil\). In Case 2 the proof assumes \(1\leq q\leq L-1\) and \(s\geq1\). Hence \(q<L\leq Ls\), so \(Ls+q<2Ls\), not \(Ls+q\geq2Ls\). The first comparison in the ensuing displayed chain is thus unsupported, and the intended exponent contradiction does not follow from that chain.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of the Banach-space stretched-exponential estimate is incomplete for all shifted indices in Case 2, although the intended estimate can be recovered by a local rearrangement once the rate constant is treated consistently.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Let \(L=\lceil2+(b-1)/s\rceil\) and \(M=Ls+q\). Replace the false comparison by \(M<2Ls\). Using the same admissible rate constant throughout the contradiction, write \(C_1\sqrt M e^{-c_1M^\alpha}<\sigma_M\leq\sigma_{Ls}\leq C_1\sqrt s e^{-c_0s^\alpha/2}\). Since \(M>s\), the square-root factor can be discarded in the favorable direction, giving \(c_1>(c_0/2)(s/M)^\alpha>(c_0/2)(2L)^{-\alpha}\), which supplies the intended contradiction.
issues.why_classification: The displayed inequality is not merely a transcriptional typo because the proof uses its wrong direction. Nevertheless, the correct inequality and the existing square-root prefactor yield a short, routine rearrangement confined to Case 2. No new lemma, proof architecture, hypothesis, convergence order, or substantive guarantee is needed, so the defect is minor.
